title: SBI and Bank of Baroda Are About to Borrow a Billion Dollars Abroad. The RBI Is Paying Part of Their Hedging Cost.
excerpt: The two state-run lenders will be the first to tap a subsidised swap window that bankers expect to pull in $15 to $20 billion over the next six months.
body:
State Bank of India and Bank of Baroda are set to become the first Indian lenders to tap the Reserve Bank of India's new subsidised hedging window for overseas borrowings, with plans to raise roughly $1 billion through five-year dollar bonds before the end of June.

The two state-run banks are each targeting around $500 million, according to three sources familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity. Both had been waiting for the RBI to formalise the facility before launching their issues.

## How the subsidy works

The RBI announced this week that external commercial borrowings with a minimum average maturity of three years by state-run companies would qualify for a swap facility at a fixed rate of 1.5 per cent per annum, compounded semi-annually. In plain terms, the central bank is absorbing a large chunk of the currency hedging cost that would normally make foreign borrowing less attractive than raising money at home.

"With 150 basis points of hedging discount, the all-in landed cost for these lenders should be around 6.25 to 6.50 per cent, which is cheaper than their local cost of borrowing," one of the sources told Reuters.

That inversion — overseas debt becoming cheaper than domestic debt — is precisely what the RBI engineered. It wants dollars flowing in, and it is willing to subsidise the mechanics to make it happen.

## Why the RBI is doing this

The measures are part of a broader salvo aimed at defending the rupee and shoring up India's balance of payments at a time when the Iran war has pushed the country's oil-and-gas import bill up by 53 per cent. Foreign investors have pulled a record $30 billion from Indian equities this year, and the rupee fell to a record low near 97 against the dollar in May before stabilising around 94.50 to 96.00.

The RBI's approach has been to attract capital through incentives rather than raising interest rates aggressively. Alongside the swap facility for overseas borrowings, it has fully subsidised hedging costs on foreign currency non-resident (FCNR) deposits with three-to-five-year maturities raised until September 30. State Bank of India alone expects inflows exceeding $34 billion from this NRI deposit route.

## $15 to $20 billion expected

Merchant bankers expect the subsidised hedging window to channel $15 to $20 billion in overseas borrowings over the next six months. SBI raised $500 million through five-year dollar bonds in September 2025 at a coupon of 4.50 per cent. It also has dollar bond maturities worth about $750 million coming up later this month and in July. Bank of Baroda currently has no outstanding dollar debt.

The broader impact is already visible in domestic markets. Corporate bond yields have fallen 40 to 45 basis points since the RBI's announcements, with AAA-rated borrowing costs for up to five years dropping sharply. Companies including Bajaj Finance, Muthoot Finance, Bajaj Housing Finance and L&T Finance have lined up bond issuances totalling over 147 billion rupees.

HSBC estimates that the full package of RBI measures could improve India's balance of payments by roughly $30 billion — cutting the projected deficit from $65 billion to around $35 billion for the fiscal year.

## What NRIs should watch

For the diaspora, the RBI's moves create a tangible opportunity. The subsidised FCNR window means banks can offer NRIs significantly higher returns on dollar deposits — some are already advertising rates above 7 per cent — because the central bank is bearing the hedging cost that would otherwise eat into yields.

But there is a deadline. The facility runs until September 30, 2026. After that, the economics change unless the RBI extends the window. NRIs weighing whether to park dollars in Indian banks have a narrow window where the maths is unusually favourable.
